article_content: It's the season of brackets, beer, and basketball. As the NCAA Tournament heats up in mid-March, fans across the country are glued to the action, eagerly awaiting the national champion crowned on April 6. More than a century after James Naismith invented the game at a YMCA in Springfield, Massachusetts, college basketball remains a powerful cultural force — uniting communities, inspiring decades-long loyalties, and turning campuses into electric arenas. With insights from the NCAA, CNN highlights five iconic college basketball towns where passion runs deep and traditions run thick. 1. Durham and Chapel Hill, North Carolina — Home to Duke and the University of North Carolina, this rivalry is legendary. Duke’s Cameron Crazies camp out for months in Krzyzewskiville — named after 12-time National Coach of the Year Mike Krzyzewski — just to secure a spot in the student section. In Chapel Hill, Tar Heel pride is woven into daily life. Locals like Adam Lucas, who skipped school as a kid to attend games, say basketball isn’t just a sport — it’s the heartbeat of the town. Don’t miss the 8,000-square-foot Carolina Basketball Museum, packed with interactive exhibits and memorabilia. 2. Lawrence, Kansas — Allen Fieldhouse, built in the 1950s and named after coaching legend Phog Allen, pulses with energy every game night. The deafening 'Rock Chalk Jayhawk' chant and student antics targeting rivals like Missouri make it one of the loudest venues in college sports. Even if you can’t snag a ticket, the Booth Family Hall of Athletics offers a deep dive into KU’s storied past. And when Kansas won the 2022 title, over 100,000 fans flooded Massachusetts Street — proof that basketball here isn’t just watched, it’s celebrated. 3. Bloomington, Indiana — Though the Hoosiers struggled this season (6-25) following the resignation of coach Kelvin Sampson, basketball remains sacred in Indiana. With five NCAA titles and the legendary Bobby Knight at the helm for decades, Assembly Hall — one of the nation’s largest student sections — still fills to capacity. Fans flock to Nick’s English Hut and Yogi’s Grill and Bar, where walls are adorned with Hoosiers gear. As student journalist Zach Osterman says, 'Basketball is a religion here.' 4. Milwaukee, Wisconsin — With no football team, Marquette’s basketball fans are even more devoted. The Superfans arrive up to 10 hours early with sleeping bags to claim front-row seats. Their creative costumes and celebrity cutouts add flair to the game-day experience. Though the Golden Eagles were eliminated last week, they now play at the Fiserv Forum — home of the NBA’s Milwaukee Bucks — not the outdated Bradley Center. Fans pack downtown Milwaukee’s Water Street on game nights, where sports bars and taverns buzz with energy. 5. Spokane, Washington — Gonzaga University, a small Jesuit school, has made the NCAA Tournament for 11 consecutive years — a feat few expected. Dubbed the 'Gonzaga Effect,' this consistency has turned the Bulldogs into March darlings. Seeded No. 4 this year, they play in the state-of-the-art McCarthey Athletic Center, replacing a former high school-style gym. The Kennel Club, their raucous student section, boasts a win rate above 75% over 17 years. Fans gather at Jack & Dan’s Tavern, owned by NBA legend John Stockton, and the popular The Bulldog burger joint. Next March, Spokane will host the first and second rounds — expected to inject $2.75 million into the local economy.

article_content: Last weekend, 'Super Saturday' saw a record 700 property auctions held across Australia, continuing a trend of soaring prices for properties in poor condition. The day might more accurately be called 'Super Expensive Saturday,' as several homes sold for top dollar despite being structurally unsound — some even uninhabitable. One such property in Balmain East, located at 3 James Lane, was visibly deteriorating when it went under the hammer — yet still fetched $2.68 million, $830,000 above its reserve price. The residence, described by the agent as a 'blank canvas' offering 'the opportunity of a lifetime for the astute and imaginative buyer,' lacked a functional kitchen and bathroom. 'It certainly wasn't liveable,' a Belle Property agent told Fairfax Media. Nevertheless, panoramic views of Sydney Harbour convinced multiple buyers to bid aggressively. The property was purchased by local 'downsizers' who plan to invest a further $600,000 in renovations before moving in. The trend extended to other properties, including a former warehouse at 164–166 Wilson Street, Newtown, which sold for $1,725,000 on Monday. The building, previously occupied by squatters who reportedly threatened the new owners, had been purchased for just $68,000 in 1981 and left unrenovated until last week. New owners intend to convert the structure into two 10-metre-wide family homes with parallel driveways. The real estate agent did not disclose the reserve price but confirmed it was significantly lower than the sale price. In Millers Point, several public housing properties also sold well above reserve, despite visible disrepair — including aged floorboards and peeling paint. The first listed, 11 Lower Fort Street, sold for $3.95 million — $1.25 million above the revised asking price. The second, 23 Lower Fort Street, sold for $2,685,000 — $985,000 above its revised asking price. These extraordinary figures reflect what housing analysts describe as a persistent price bubble. Peter Kelahar, Director of PK Property, told Daily Mail Australia that limited housing supply is driving demand and inflating valuations. He added that many agents are preparing to launch listings after the October long weekend: 'They're ready to flick the switch. They have all the photos taken and are just waiting for the right time.' 'At the moment, it's a bit of a Mexican standoff — people won't list unless they’ve secured another place to live. It’ll loosen eventually, but be aware of the trends.'

'Non era assolutamente abitabile,' ha dichiarato un agente di Belle Property a Fairfax Media. La proprietà è stata acquistata da 'downsizers' locali che prevedono di investire altri 600.000 dollari in ristrutturazioni prima di trasferirsi. Ha aggiunto che molti agenti stanno preparando i lanci dopo il ponte di ottobre: 'Sono pronti ad accendere l'interruttore. Hanno tutte le foto pronte e stanno solo aspettando il momento giusto.' 'Al momento è un po' uno scontro a distanza — le persone non mettono in vendita se non hanno già trovato un altro posto dove vivere. Alla fine si sbloccherà, ma state attenti alle tendenze.'

article_content: Actress Angela Lansbury, 88, was made a Dame by Queen Elizabeth II in a ceremony at Windsor Castle, honoring her lifelong contributions to drama and charity. Still performing on London’s West End, Lansbury expressed deep pride in being recognized by her country of birth — Britain — despite having moved to the United States as a child. She joins an elite group of acting Dames, including Judi Dench and Penelope Keith. Lansbury’s illustrious career spans seven decades: she earned three Oscar nominations for roles in Gaslight (1944), The Picture of Dorian Gray (1945), and The Manchurian Candidate (1962); won five Tony Awards and six Golden Globes; received an honorary Oscar last year; and is best known globally as Jessica Fletcher in Murder, She Wrote. Last month, she returned to the London stage for the first time in nearly 40 years, reprising her Tony-winning role in Noel Coward’s Blithe Spirit at the Gielgud Theatre. Also honored at the ceremony were veteran entertainer Nicholas Parsons, 90, who received a CBE for his decades of service to children’s charities — a recognition that follows his 2013 OBE for broadcasting. Parsons remarked, 'It is very nice to be honoured for all the things you do because you enjoy and love them.' He shared that the Queen commended his hard work as 'greatly admired.' Rifleman Michael Swain, 24, walked unaided on advanced bionic prosthetics to receive his MBE after losing both legs in a Taliban bomb blast in Afghanistan in 2009. Following groundbreaking osseointegration surgery in Australia — where titanium rods were fused to his thigh bones — Swain can now attach his prosthetic limbs in seconds. Despite fears of stumbling before the Queen, he successfully collected his medal, joking afterward that he couldn’t wait to swap his uniform shoes for trainers. His partner, Jade Hardiman, praised his resilience as a father to their three-year-old son and their unborn daughter. Sculptor Antony Gormley was knighted for services to the arts, accepting the honor 'in the name of sculpture.' Known for iconic works like the Angel of the North and Another Place, Gormley emphasized sculpture’s unique ability to engage the public imagination. He also honored the late Sir Anthony Caro and noted the Queen’s role in strengthening UK-Ireland relations, recalling how she introduced him at a recent state banquet as 'the sculptor, he makes enormous things.'

article_content: To mark the centenary of the First World War, the UK government is launching a sweeping £50 million commemorative initiative spanning five years, designed to ensure the sacrifices of a generation are never forgotten. Central to this effort is a £5.3 million program that will send two students and a teacher from every state-funded secondary school in Britain to walk the hallowed ground of battlefields like the Somme, Verdun, and Fromelles. These educational journeys, set to begin in spring 2014 and continue through 2019, aim to forge a personal, emotional connection between young people and the war’s enduring legacy. Prime Minister David Cameron, speaking at the Imperial War Museum, stressed that the Great War isn’t just a chapter in history books — it shaped modern Britain. He pointed to how it accelerated women’s rights, improved medical care, and spurred greater recognition for minority communities. ‘This matters — not just in our heads, but in our hearts,’ he said, referencing his own deep personal connection to the war through Robert Graves’ memoir, Goodbye to All That. Defence Minister Andrew Murrison emphasized that the commemorations will focus solely on remembrance, avoiding any glorification or political debate. ‘Millions died. The consequences are still with us,’ he noted. Similarly, the Royal British Legion highlighted how loss touched every corner of the UK, with memorials in nearly every village and town serving as quiet testaments to grief. National events will center around key dates: the outbreak of war on August 4, 2014; the first day of the Somme on July 1, 2016; and the Armistice centenary in 2018. Additional initiatives include £15 million in community grants for local projects — such as football matches reenacting the 1914 Christmas Truce — and £5 million toward upgrading the Imperial War Museum’s WW1 exhibits. A further £1 million will preserve HMS Caroline, the last surviving British warship from the era. In a notable misstep, Cameron mistakenly claimed 200,000 British troops died in one day at the Somme — the actual figure was 20,000. This follows earlier public errors, including misidentifying the composer of Rule Britannia and misstating the meaning of Magna Carta. Despite these gaffes, the broader commemorative plan has drawn cross-party support, particularly following the 2009 funeral of Harry Patch, the last known British veteran of the trenches.

Ha indicato come abbia accelerato i diritti delle donne, migliorato le cure mediche e spinto un maggior riconoscimento per le minoranze etniche. 'Questo conta — non solo nella nostra mente, ma nel nostro cuore,' ha detto, riferendosi al suo profondo legame personale con la guerra attraverso le memorie di Robert Graves, Addio a tutto ciò. Gli eventi nazionali si concentreranno su date chiave: l'inizio della guerra il 4 agosto 2014; il primo giorno della Somme il 1° luglio 2016; e il centenario dell'Armistizio nel 2018. Ulteriori iniziative includono 15 milioni di sterline in sovvenzioni comunitarie per progetti locali — come partite di calcio che rievocano l'armistizio natalizio del 1914 — e 5 milioni di sterline per l'aggiornamento delle gallerie della Prima Guerra Mondiale al Museo dell'Impero della Guerra. Nonostante questi sbagli, il piano commemorativo più ampio ha ricevuto sostegno trasversale, specialmente dopo il funerale del 2009 di Harry Patch, l'ultimo veterano britannico noto delle trincee.

article_content: The Australian Defence Force (ADF) is facing allegations that the 2nd Battalion of the Royal Australian Regiment (2 RAR) paid four civilian women to perform topless at an Oktoberfest event held on September 26 at The Booza — the Edgar Towner Victoria Cross Club at Lavarack Barracks in Townsville, Queensland. Despite explicit orders from Lieutenant Colonel Michael Bassingthwaighte prohibiting such conduct, the women were reportedly paid to remove their clothing during the gathering, which included over 100 soldiers and junior officers, a roast pig, and $6,000 worth of alcohol. A post on the battalion’s official Facebook page, '2 RAR Pipes and Drums,' celebrated the event with the caption: 'The Pig carcass destroyed. Two cartons left out of the 6G we spent on booze. One fat lip. One possible demotion. BUT ONE HELL OF A NIGHT!' One commenter wrote, 'You wouldn’t have it any other way.' The ADF stated that written and verbal instructions had been issued requiring bar staff to remain fully clothed. The women, reportedly freelance workers recommended by a battalion member rather than through official channels, allegedly violated these directives. The corporal responsible for organizing the event was demoted and sentenced to 14 days’ detention. However, a subsequent review concluded that Lieutenant Colonel Bassingthwaighte could not impartially adjudicate charges related to his own orders, leading to the corporal’s reinstatement and the overturning of the punishment. Photos published by ninemsn showed soldiers alongside topless women, including one with tattoos and blonde hair, and another with pink nail polish giving a peace sign. The ADF has faced multiple similar scandals in recent years, including incidents at the SASR barracks in Swanbourne, Western Australia, where government-owned bars had previously employed topless staff before being banned. Separately, ABC TV’s Four Corners program featured testimonies from four former female cadets who claimed they were raped, sexually assaulted, or degraded at the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA) during the 1990s and 2009. They criticized the Defence Abuse Response Taskforce as ineffective. Advocates including former ADF magistrate Ken Northwood, Senator Jacqui Lambie, and lawyer Gary Rumble are urging a royal commission to fully investigate systemic abuse within the military.

Le donne, presumibilmente lavoratrici autonome raccomandate da un membro del battaglione piuttosto che attraverso canali ufficiali, avrebbero violato tali direttive. Il caporale responsabile dell'organizzazione dell'evento è stato degradato e condannato a 14 giorni di detenzione. Tuttavia, una successiva revisione ha concluso che il Tenente Colonnello Bassingthwaighte non poteva giudicare imparzialmente accuse relative ai suoi stessi ordini, portando alla riabilitazione del caporale e all'annullamento della punizione. Foto pubblicate da ninemsn mostrano soldati insieme a donne topless, tra cui una con tatuaggi e capelli biondi, e un'altra con smalto rosa che fa il segno della pace. L'ADF ha affrontato numerosi scandali simili negli ultimi anni, inclusi casi presso la base del Special Air Service Regiment (SASR) a Swanbourne, nell'Australia Occidentale, dove bar gestite dal governo avevano precedentemente impiegato donne topless prima di essere bandite. Separatamente, il programma Four Corners della ABC TV ha presentato testimonianze di quattro ex cadette femminili che affermano di essere state violentate, assalite sessualmente o umiliate all'Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA) negli anni '90 e nel 2009. Hanno criticato la Defence Abuse Response Taskforce come inefficace. Avvocati e sostenitori tra cui l'ex magistrato ADF Ken Northwood, la senatrice Jacqui Lambie e l'avvocato Gary Rumble chiedono una commissione reale per indagare a fondo gli abusi sistematici all'interno delle forze armate.

article_content: The Federal Communications Commission has ruled that using the term 'Redskins' on radio broadcasts does not constitute profanity, dismissing a petition that sought to strip a Washington-area station of its license. The petition, filed by law professor John Banzhaf, argued that repeated use of the word violated indecency standards. However, the FCC explained that federal law defines profanity narrowly — limited to language involving sex or bodily functions — neither of which applies to the team’s name. The decision protects WWXX-FM, a station owned by team owner Dan Snyder. Despite widespread criticism from Native American communities and civil rights advocates who call 'Redskins' a harmful racial slur, Snyder has repeatedly refused to change the name, even amid mounting pressure from lawmakers, including 50 U.S. senators who urged him to act earlier this year. In a related development, the U.S. Patent Office revoked the team’s trademarks last spring, though that ruling is currently being challenged in court. According to a report by Patrick Hruby of Sports on Earth, rebranding the franchise could cost between $10 and $20 million — a figure that pales in comparison to the annual salaries of some NFL stars, yet carries deep cultural significance beyond financial metrics.

La petizione, presentata dal professore di diritto John Banzhaf, sosteneva che l'uso ripetuto della parola violasse le norme sull'indecenza. Tuttavia, la FCC ha chiarito che la legge federale definisce il linguaggio osceno in modo ristretto — limitato alle parole relative a sesso o funzioni corporee — nessuna delle quali si applica al nome della squadra. article_content: In Moreno Valley, California, a three-year-old pit bull named Huey was discovered abandoned, barely alive — skeletal, covered in bite marks, and suffering from severe malnutrition. Animal rescuers believe he was used as live bait in a dogfighting operation, with his lips torn and his mouth taped shut to prevent him from defending himself. When found, he weighed only 33 pounds and was infested with parasites, with infected ears and a jaw so badly damaged it could not be repaired. His condition was so dire that many thought he wouldn’t survive the night. Huey was taken in by Second Chance Rescue in Corona, where he received emergency treatment. After weeks of intensive care, he was adopted by Tracy Lystra, who has dedicated herself to his recovery. In the first 12 hours with her, Huey vomited repeatedly and suffered violent diarrhea — moments she spent sleeping beside him, whispering encouragement. Against all odds, he began to heal. Today, Huey shows steady improvement. His wounds are closing, his energy is returning, and he even dreams, whimpers, and shakes in his sleep — signs, Lystra says, that he’s processing trauma and beginning to trust again. 'To me, he’s a miracle,' she told KTLA 5. Lystra has created a Facebook page called 'Saving Huey' to document his journey and raise awareness about the brutality of dogfighting. She hopes his story will inspire others to speak up and protect vulnerable animals. So far, donations through Give Forward have totaled $1,325 to cover his medical bills.

article_content: In a televised interview, Hezbollah’s leader Hassan Nasrallah issued a stark warning: if Israel launches an attack on Iran’s nuclear infrastructure, Iran could retaliate by striking U.S. military installations across the Middle East. Nasrallah claimed this response strategy was approved by Iranian authorities and emphasized that America would share blame if Israel moves forward. He added that he doesn’t believe Israel will launch such an attack in the near term, citing internal divisions within the Israeli government. Iran has previously demonstrated its missile capabilities, with senior military officials stating that U.S. bases in the Gulf — including the U.S. Navy’s 5th Fleet in Bahrain — lie within range of Iranian ballistic missiles. In July 2012, Iran announced it could neutralize these bases and hit Israel within minutes of any strike against its territory. It also revealed successful tests of anti-ship missiles capable of sinking American warships in the Persian Gulf. Meanwhile, Israel’s largest newspaper, Yedioth Ahronoth, reported that the U.S. had secretly engaged Iran through European intermediaries to secure a pledge that Tehran would avoid targeting American forces in the event of an Israeli strike. The report offered no verifiable sources and was quickly dismissed by Israeli officials as implausible. The White House declined to comment, as the story broke over the Labor Day holiday. Amid rising tensions, U.S. officials reaffirmed their unwavering commitment to Israel’s security and to stopping Iran from obtaining nuclear weapons. White House spokesman Jay Carney stressed there is 'no daylight' between Washington and Jerusalem on this issue. Israeli Deputy Prime Minister Dan Meridor echoed this, saying Iran understands the catastrophic consequences of crossing a nuclear threshold — including overwhelming U.S. military retaliation. However, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu criticized the Obama administration for what he sees as insufficient pressure on Iran, urging global powers to establish a clear, publicly declared 'red line' for Iran’s nuclear program. He argued that diplomatic efforts and sanctions have failed to deter Tehran, a sentiment widely interpreted as a veiled rebuke of U.S. policy. General Martin Dempsey, meanwhile, expressed reluctance to be involved if Israel chooses military action — highlighting growing strategic unease even among top U.S. military leaders.

article_content: HP has unveiled a bold new initiative called HP ePrint — a system that lets users print from any device simply by sending an email to a uniquely assigned printer address. No drivers needed. Just send, and it prints. Built on the foundation of Google Cloud Print, introduced earlier this year, HP ePrint enables direct cloud connectivity via touchscreen interfaces. Users can now print Google Docs, scan directly to Google Drive, and even print photos from Picasa or calendar events — all without touching a computer. The platform also supports third-party cloud services such as Box.net and Docstoc, letting users pull and push documents seamlessly. Beyond productivity, HP is exploring innovative uses like scheduled printing: Imagine waking up to a personalized daily newspaper printed and waiting for you on the kitchen counter. MSNBC has partnered with HP to pilot this feature, while Yahoo handles the ad placement — delivering targeted local promotions and coupons. For developers, HP has opened its SDK to build apps that turn printing into new experiences: print Facebook photos, MapQuest directions, Crayola coloring pages for kids, or PBS educational worksheets. With tens of millions of web-connected printers expected to ship next year, the opportunity is significant. At its core, HP’s move isn’t just about selling hardware — it’s about reigniting ink demand. As digital alternatives replace traditional print tasks like coupons and boarding passes, HP needs new reasons for people to keep using printers. Web-connected, email-enabled printers offer exactly that: frictionless, everyday use cases that bring users back to physical output. HP is showcasing these innovations at its press event kicking off Internet Week New York, where a panel featuring key partners will discuss the future of connected printing. Disclosure: HP sponsors Mashable’s coverage of Internet Week New York.

article_content: In the western Venezuelan city of San Cristóbal, 14-year-old Kluibert Roa Nuñez was fatally shot by a national police officer just blocks from his school — a tragedy that has deepened the nation’s political rift. According to multiple eyewitnesses, Kluibert was not protesting; he was simply walking home from class when chaos erupted around him. As students fled from police, he ducked under a car for safety — only to be struck by a bullet fired directly by Officer Javier Mora Ortiz. The government swiftly responded, naming Mora as the shooter and charging him with intentional homicide, while also arresting nine protesters. Yet, Kluibert’s parents remain unconvinced. His father, Erick Roa, doubts the official account: he questions whether the weapon used was truly loaded with rubber pellets, as claimed, or lethal lead rounds. Witnesses also contradict the government’s assertion that medical aid was rendered promptly. Meanwhile, protests have flared again across Venezuela, with students in Caracas holding up red-smeared notebooks as symbols of their silenced voices. 'These are our weapons,' one protester declared, 'notebooks, pens, thoughts.' The Maduro administration insists this was an isolated act by a rogue officer and not representative of its police force — a force it claims has been reformed into a more humanist, rights-respecting institution. But with Venezuela enduring severe economic collapse — chronic shortages of food, medicine, and even toilet paper, alongside a currency in freefall — many see the killing as part of a larger pattern of repression. Just days before, opposition leader and Caracas mayor Antonio Ledezma was arrested, fueling accusations that the government is using violence and detention to distract from its failing economy. Social media has exploded with opposing hashtags: #MaduroAsesinoDeEstudiantes versus #ApoyoRotundoAMaduro, revealing a country deeply divided — and grieving.

article_content: The tension between Sebastian Vettel and Mark Webber reached a boiling point at the Malaysian Grand Prix, when Vettel disregarded team instructions to pass his teammate and claim victory. The move reignited years of simmering friction within Red Bull, with Webber left to process not just the loss, but what he sees as a pattern of preferential treatment. In the aftermath, Webber told reporters he’d be heading to the beach — surfing to clear his head and reflect on his place in the team. He hinted that the incident wasn’t isolated, pointing to past clashes, including the infamous 2010 Turkish GP crash that left lasting resentment. While Red Bull boss Christian Horner publicly downplayed the drama, insisting the team remains united, insiders know Webber has long been the junior partner. Vettel, closely mentored by Helmut Marko — a powerful figure tied to team owner Dietrich Mateschitz — has enjoyed consistent backing, something Webber hasn’t shared. After the race, Webber remarked bitterly that Vettel ‘made his own decisions and will have protection as usual.’ Horner acknowledged the fallout, saying the matter would be addressed internally, even as he reiterated his commitment to supporting both drivers equally. Critics, including ex-driver John Watson, weren’t convinced. Watson argued that Horner had lost control and suggested suspending Vettel for one race to restore order. Meanwhile, Vettel offered a mea culpa, calling the overtake a mistake and saying he’d undo it if he could. Yet, the controversy isn’t just personal — it’s systemic. Team orders, once banned in F1, have quietly returned, and this time, they’re being applied unevenly: while Vettel defied them, Hamilton was allowed to coast to a podium after Rosberg was told not to push. The sport now faces a deeper question: when does strategy become favoritism?

article_content: On January 16, 2014, Dennis McGuire, a 53-year-old death row inmate in Ohio, became the first person in the United States to be executed using a novel combination of two drugs: midazolam, a sedative, and hydromorphone, a powerful painkiller. His death took 26 minutes — the longest in Ohio since capital punishment resumed in 1999 — and was marked by audible gasps and convulsions. Family members who witnessed the event described it as torture, sparking national debate over the humanity of lethal injection protocols. In the days following, allegations surfaced that McGuire’s attorney, Robert Lowe, had urged him to exaggerate signs of distress during the procedure in hopes of galvanizing public opposition to the death penalty. According to state prison records, McGuire reportedly told correctional officers that he refused to ‘put on a show’ for his kids or anyone’s agenda. ‘It’s about me and my children, not him and his cause,’ he allegedly said. The Ohio Public Defender’s Office responded by suspending Lowe briefly, then reinstating him after reviewing the claims. Spokesperson Amy Borror emphasized that no staff from their office were present during the execution to prevent even the appearance of interference. She clarified that Lowe had simply explained the process to McGuire — including asking him to raise a thumbs-up once he felt unconscious — and that McGuire’s remarks might have stemmed from misunderstanding those instructions. Medical experts noted that the combination of midazolam and hydromorphone can trigger a sensation known as ‘air hunger’ — a terrifying feeling of inability to breathe — even in healthy individuals under high doses. This effect may explain McGuire’s physical reactions, rather than intentional theatrics. Ohio adopted this drug regimen after European manufacturers stopped supplying pentobarbital, the previous drug of choice, for use in executions. With the legality and ethics of the new protocol now under scrutiny, officials are expected to reassess its future use.

article_content: NEW YORK (CNN) — Chesley B. 'Sully' Sullenberger III was 'the right guy at the right time in the right moment' to guide US Airways Flight 1549 safely onto the Hudson River, said a neighbor and longtime friend. A U.S. Air Force veteran and seasoned pilot with over four decades of experience, Sullenberger has been with US Airways since 1980. Known for his calm, composed demeanor — shaped by years of flying and deep research into aviation safety — he exemplified precision under pressure. All 155 passengers and crew aboard the Airbus A320 survived the January 15, 2009, emergency water landing following a double bird strike that disabled both engines. Passengers credited the flight attendants for maintaining order: repeatedly chanting 'brace, brace, brace' as the plane descended, ensuring everyone remained secured and in position. Co-pilot Jeffrey Skiles, 49, later praised the swift response of local rescue boats. 'He was really grateful and impressed by how quickly help arrived,' said his wife, Barbara Skiles. Sullenberger’s career is marked by distinction: graduate of the Air Force Academy in 1973, former F-4 Phantom fighter pilot, flight leader, and mission commander for elite Red Flag combat training exercises. He has served as a safety chairman for the Air Line Pilots Association, accident investigator, and collaborator with NASA and the National Transportation Safety Board on aviation safety research. He is president and CEO of Safety Reliability Methods Inc., a firm advising the aviation industry on risk management and emergency protocols. His actions after the landing — walking the cabin twice to confirm no one was left behind — earned widespread acclaim. Lt. Gen. John Regni, his classmate at the Air Force Academy, called it the embodiment of 'service before self.' New York Mayor Michael Bloomberg commended Sullenberger’s mastery of the landing and his meticulous post-crash checks. 'He made sure everybody got out,' Bloomberg said. Sullenberger’s wife, Lorrie, described him as 'a pilot’s pilot' — deeply devoted to the craft and unshakably professional. 'This is the Sully I know,' she told CNN. 'It’s not unusual. It’s just who he is.' Despite global praise, Sullenberger remained quiet in the immediate aftermath, focused on recovery and ensuring his family’s safety.

article_content: This summer, Bournemouth kept a tight rein on transfer spending—but manager Eddie Howe knows the board stands firmly behind him if he decides to make big moves later. After a surprise 10th-place finish in the Championship last season—sparked by a modest £2.5 million investment in players like Tokelo Rantie—the club has shifted focus to internal growth. Howe says the decision to scale back was his own, not forced by ownership. With the team preparing for a match against Huddersfield, confidence is high that they can push for a playoff spot. Howe believes their current squad, averaging a young and promising age, is stronger than ever. While they lost top scorer Lewis Grabban to Norwich for £3 million, they wisely used part of that money to bring in 22-year-old Callum Wilson from Coventry. For Howe, this isn't just a transfer; it's a statement. Bournemouth has built its identity on nurturing talent rather than splurging on stars. 'If you can't find someone better than what you already have, why spend?' he says. 'Development beats acquisition when you're working with limited resources.' This philosophy has roots in the club’s turbulent past: two bankruptcies in 1997 and 2008, before owner Maxim Demin stepped in to rebuild. Now, with financial stability restored, Howe credits consistent dialogue with the board for their rise. When asked if funds will be available in January to chase a top-six finish, he replied confidently: 'They've never said no to me on a signing. When the moment comes, I know they'll back us.'

article_content: On Monday night and early Tuesday, many Californians were jolted awake by piercing, screeching sounds coming from their phones — it wasn’t a fire alarm or a prank. It was California’s first-ever statewide Amber Alert, triggered by the abduction of 8-year-old Ethan Anderson and his 16-year-old sister, Hannah. The alert, part of a new federal system rolled out at the end of 2012, broadcasts emergency notifications directly to nearby mobile devices using a high-pitched tone meant to grab attention — no matter where you are or whether you signed up. This isn’t the first time Amber Alerts have reached phones — since 2005, users could voluntarily subscribe and pick regions to monitor. But that system was flawed: if you were visiting Florida while living in Nebraska, you wouldn’t get alerts for local emergencies. Now, thanks to FEMA’s Wireless Emergency Alert program, your phone responds to your physical location, not your area code. If you’re near a threat, you get the alert — period. Some, like Marc Klaas — whose daughter Polly was tragically killed in a 1993 kidnapping — worry the startling noise might turn people off. 'It’s well-intentioned,' he told CNN, 'but the rollout was pretty abysmal.' He fears many will disable the feature altogether. Still, the system has proven effective. In February, a Minnesota teen spotted an Amber Alert describing a Kia matching a neighbor’s car. He called police — and saved an 8-month-old baby. Since then, over 100 such alerts have been sent nationwide, with carriers covering 98% of U.S. phones. Even older devices like the iPhone 4 won’t receive them, but most modern smartphones do. The alert that shook California offered little detail — just a description of a blue Nissan. Critics called it too vague. But as columnist Jon Healey pointed out in the LA Times, police often don’t know where the abductor is heading. To catch them, you need to reach everyone possible. The goal isn’t convenience — it’s survival. And while the noise is loud, it’s intentional. Unlike regular texts, these alerts use Cell Broadcast, a dedicated channel immune to network overload. You can silence them in your phone’s settings — but you’ll have to opt out. Because when seconds count, this system doesn’t wait for permission.

article_content: Federal reports have revealed that terrorists would need to sabotage only nine out of the 55,000 electric transmission substations across the U.S. to cause a national blackout lasting more than a year. A coast-to-coast blackout has become a harrowing yet plausible threat, prompting federal regulators to issue warnings and call for widespread security upgrades. The Wall Street Journal published findings from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), explaining how attacks on select substations could disable all three major U.S. power grids. The U.S. energy grid consists of three largely isolated systems, meaning that targeting just nine key substations—and one transformer manufacturer—could shut down the entire network for at least 18 months, possibly longer. In a June memo recently made public, FERC’s Director of External Affairs, Leonard Tao, wrote: 'Destroy nine interconnection substations and a transformer manufacturer, and the entire United States grid would be down for at least 18 months, probably longer.' The challenge isn’t limited to just nine stations: approximately 30 substations meet the criteria for critical impact, and fewer than a third of those would need to be compromised to trigger a collapse. Experts disagree on the exact number—some estimate closer to 100—but all agree on the severity of the risk. 'It is neither a monumental task nor an inordinate sum of money that would be required to do so,' said former FERC Chairman Jon Wellinghoff in an email to the Wall Street Journal. Currently, federal law focuses security requirements on nuclear power plants, not conventional electricity infrastructure. Concerns intensified after an April 2013 attack on a PG&E substation in San Jose, California, where one or two individuals shot 17 transformers in under 20 minutes, severed fiber-optic communication lines, and escaped before police arrived. Although no one was injured and the local grid remained operational due to backup systems, officials believe the attack was a carefully planned reconnaissance or test run. 'This wasn’t an incident where Billy-Bob and Joe decided, after a few brewskis, to come in and shoot up a substation,' said Mark Johnson, retired VP of Transmission for PG&E. Surveillance footage released by the Santa Clara Sheriff’s Office showed the attackers firing at equipment, sparks flying as transformers were damaged. Four Democratic senators—Dianne Feinstein (CA), Harry Reid (NV), Ron Wyden (OR), and Al Franken (MN)—sent a letter to federal regulators in February, urging mandatory physical security standards for substations. They called the attack a 'wake-up call to the risk of physical attacks on the grid,' noting it came 'uncomfortably close to causing a massive blackout in California and elsewhere in the West.' While federal cybersecurity standards for the grid are mandatory, physical protection measures—such as fencing, surveillance, and armed guards—are still voluntary for private utility operators.

Hanno definito l'attacco un 'campanello d'allarme sul rischio di attacchi fisici alla rete', osservando che era 'venuto troppo vicino a causare un grande black-out in California e altrove nell'Ovest.' article_content: The UK’s automatic £100 penalty for filing income tax returns even one day late is under review — after HMRC admitted it’s unfairly hitting honest taxpayers who simply made a mistake. Right now, someone who files 24 hours late pays the same fine as someone who ignores the deadline for months. That’s why HMRC is proposing a major overhaul: ditching the flat fee and introducing a system similar to driving penalty points, where only repeat offenders face serious consequences. The idea? Reward good-faith errors and target those who consistently dodge their responsibilities. Last year, hundreds of thousands of middle-income families were suddenly thrust into the world of self-assessment after changes to child benefit rules. Many struggled with the confusing forms, forgot deadlines, or were new to the process — and got slapped with fines regardless of whether they owed any tax. Currently, HMRC only accepts extreme reasons for delays like bereavement or hospitalization. But officials now say that list might need updating to reflect real-life challenges. What’s more, the £100 fine kicks in even if you don’t owe a penny — a policy that existed until 2012 but was reinstated. Critics argue this turns tax compliance into a revenue grab, not a fairness tool. Chas Roy-Chowdhury from ACCA says taxpayers are essentially unpaid tax administrators — and the system should help them succeed, not punish them for slip-ups. Instead of fines, HMRC is also exploring charging interest on overdue amounts — a nudge to pay sooner without the stigma of a penalty. And while some worry removing automatic fines might reduce urgency, others believe fairer rules actually encourage long-term compliance. As HMRC opens the plan to public feedback, the goal is clear: build a system that punishes dishonesty, not human error.

article_content: A recent federal study led by NOAA has concluded that the devastating 2012 drought across the Great Plains was primarily driven by natural atmospheric conditions—not human-induced climate change. According to researchers, a breakdown in the usual flow of moist air from the Gulf of Mexico during late spring, combined with unusually sparse summer storms, created the perfect recipe for extreme dryness. The drought, which affected six states—Wyoming, Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska, South Dakota, and North Dakota—was the most severe recorded since 1895, even outpacing the infamous Dust Bowl years of the 1930s. Study lead Martin Hoerling, a NOAA meteorologist, described the event as possibly occurring only once every few centuries, with no reliable early indicators to forecast it. While Hoerling affirms that global warming is real and has raised Earth’s average temperature by roughly 1°C over the past century, he insists this particular drought wasn’t triggered by rising greenhouse gas levels. 'Not every dry spell is climate change,' he emphasized. Economic damage from the drought had already hit $12 billion by mid-2012, with crop failures and disrupted river transport contributing heavily. Though comparisons to the $78 billion 1988 drought remain possible, the full financial toll is still being assessed. The study, reviewed by 20 scientists from multiple institutions, was rigorously vetted. However, climate scientist Kevin Trenberth of the National Center for Atmospheric Research challenged the findings, arguing that the report overlooked how higher baseline temperatures due to global warming worsen drought impacts—through reduced snowpack in the Southwest, intensified heatwaves, and suppressed monsoon activity. He contends that while droughts form naturally, climate change acts like fuel on the fire, making them more destructive than they otherwise would be.

article_content: Jose Mourinho has voiced his frustration over how little contact he’s received from national team coaches this season—only England’s Roy Hodgson has reached out. The Chelsea manager is particularly upset about Spain’s handling of Diego Costa, who suffered a hamstring injury during international duty and will miss Chelsea’s upcoming Champions League match against Maribor. Mourinho believes the injury could have been prevented with better communication between Spain’s medical staff and his own coaching team. Despite his disappointment, Mourinho doesn’t blame his players for answering international calls—he encourages them to represent their countries. But he’s critical of federations that treat players like disposable assets rather than valued members of both club and nation. He recalls how Croatia’s Igor Stimac used to call him multiple times a week during Modrić’s time at Real Madrid, keeping him fully informed. By contrast, Spain’s Vicente del Bosque hasn’t made a single call this season. Mourinho acknowledges there are no official rules forcing national teams to coordinate with clubs. He says the system relies entirely on goodwill—and too often, that goodwill is missing. 'It’s up to them,' he said. 'We can’t force them to call. We can’t demand updates. All we can do is hope they care.' Chelsea are dealing with a host of injuries: Costa, Mikel Obi, and Ramires are sidelined, while André Schurrle is recovering from illness—though he trained on Monday. Without Costa, either Didier Drogba or Loïc Remy will lead the attack against Maribor. Mourinho may also give Petr Cech the nod over Thibaut Courtois in goal. But he insists his focus remains firmly on Maribor—not Manchester United. The Slovenian side hasn’t lost a Champions League game this season, having held their own against Celtic, Schalke, and Sporting Lisbon. 'They’re dangerous,' Mourinho warned. 'We’re not taking them lightly.' Looking ahead, Mourinho says if he ever becomes Portugal’s national coach, he’ll make sure clubs are treated with respect—because he knows firsthand how much it matters.

article_content: Tomorrow, Bradley Wiggins could make history by becoming the first British rider to win the Tour de France, as the race concludes on Paris’s Champs-Élysées. Yet behind the triumph, a quiet storm has been brewing within Team Sky. The spark? A heated exchange on Twitter between Catherine Wiggins, Bradley’s wife, and Michelle Cound, partner of teammate Chris Froome. Cound, a South African sports photographer, took issue with what she saw as Wiggins receiving preferential treatment — particularly after Stage 11, when Froome was asked to slow down to preserve Wiggins’ lead in the yellow jersey. Cound’s initial tweet — later deleted — hinted at frustration: 'Teamwork means letting those who support you also have their moment to shine.' Catherine Wiggins replied by lauding other riders like Mick Rogers and Richie Porte for their selflessness — but notably left out Froome. That omission triggered a sharp comeback from Cound: 'I doubt many other pro cyclists’ partners understand the sport as well as I do. And I know exactly what happened back there.' She added, 'If you want loyalty, get a Froome dog — that’s a quality I value, even if others take it for granted.' Peta Todd, partner of stage winner Mark Cavendish, then entered the fray, seemingly backing Cound’s view. Despite the online friction, Wiggins remains calm, holding a two-minute, five-second lead heading into the final stage. He’s publicly backed Froome, saying, 'He’ll have his day.' At 27, Froome is widely seen as a future champion. Meanwhile, Wiggins, a three-time Olympic gold medalist, has spoken openly about his complicated bond with his Australian father — a former racer himself — adding depth to his personal journey.

article_content: On December 28, 2012, President Barack Obama issued a stark warning: if Senate leaders failed to reach a budget agreement to avert the impending fiscal cliff, he would send his own proposal to Congress for an immediate up-or-down vote. Speaking from the White House briefing room after a 65-minute meeting with congressional leaders, Obama emphasized the urgency of the moment. 'The hour for immediate action is here — it is now,' he said. 'In just four days, tax rates will rise by law for every American, and paychecks will shrink accordingly.' While describing the meeting as 'constructive,' Obama expressed only 'modest optimism' that a deal could be reached before the December 31 deadline. He sharply criticized Congress for its prolonged inaction, noting that businesses and consumers were already pulling back due to Washington's dysfunction. Obama’s plan would preserve existing tax rates for middle-class families — defined as those earning under $400,000 annually — while allowing rates to increase for higher earners. It would also extend unemployment benefits for the long-term jobless and establish a framework for future deficit reduction. The meeting included Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid, Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell, House Speaker John Boehner, and House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi — the same quartet that had met over a month earlier with hopes of compromise. Since then, negotiations have stalled. Boehner, facing rebellion within his own caucus, abandoned a last-minute Plan B that would have raised taxes only on earners above $1 million — a figure far above Obama’s $400,000 threshold. Financial markets reacted negatively. The Dow Jones Industrial Average plummeted between 3:30 and 4:00 p.m. on Friday, marking its fifth straight day of losses, as investors lost confidence in a near-term resolution. Beyond income taxes, other looming deadlines include the expiration of the Alternative Minimum Tax patch — threatening tax hikes on millions of upper-middle-class households — and steep cuts to Medicare provider payments. Additionally, federal dairy price supports are set to revert to a formula that could nearly double the price of milk. The Congressional Budget Office warns that failure to act could push unemployment above 9% and shrink GDP by 5% in a single quarter. Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke cautioned that such a shock could plunge the economy back into recession — with ripple effects across global markets.

Boehner, di fronte a una ribellione all'interno del suo gruppo, ha abbandonato un ultimo piano B che avrebbe aumentato le tasse solo sui redditi superiori a 1 milione di dollari — un importo molto superiore alla proposta di Obama di 400.000 dollari. I mercati finanziari hanno reagito negativamente. L'Indice Industriale Dow Jones è crollato tra le 15:30 e le 16:00 di venerdì, segnando il quinto giorno consecutivo di perdite, mentre gli investitori perdevano fiducia in una risoluzione a breve termine. Oltre alle aliquote sul reddito, altre scadenze imminenti includono la scadenza del provvedimento sull'Alternative Minimum Tax — che minaccia aumenti fiscali per milioni di famiglie della classe media alta — e tagli drastici ai pagamenti ai fornitori di Medicare. Inoltre, i sostegni federali ai prezzi del latte sono destinati a tornare a una formula che potrebbe quasi raddoppiare il prezzo del latte. L'Ufficio del Bilancio del Congresso avverte che il mancato intervento potrebbe spingere la disoccupazione oltre il 9% e ridurre il PIL del 5% in un singolo trimestre. Il presidente della Federal Reserve Ben Bernanke ha avvertito che un tale shock potrebbe spingere l'economia nuovamente in recessione — con effetti a catena su tutto il sistema finanziario globale.

article_content: For more than a century, the historic clock at Victoria Hall in Ash, Surrey, has marked time with chimes every 15 minutes—day and night. But now, its nighttime chimes are being silenced following a complaint from a couple who moved into the house next door. The decision, criticized by Communities Secretary Eric Pickles as a 'politically correct health-and-safety purge,' has prompted new national guidance for councils to protect long-standing community sounds. Legal expert Steve Tai, 44, and his accountant wife Yong Wong, 41, moved to Ash last September from a nearby village. After purchasing their home for £295,950 following a single viewing, Tai complained to the Victoria Hall management trust that the clock’s chimes disrupted their sleep and caused depression. The trust, advised it would likely lose a legal case, purchased a bespoke timer for £1,700 plus installation fees to mute the chimes between 11pm and 7am. Despite the decision, villagers rallied to raise funds to cover the cost, expressing anger that a decades-old tradition could be overturned by a single complaint. David Brown of the hall’s management committee said: 'There's a lot of resentment that someone can come into a place and stop something that's been going on for 100 years without any real feel for the community in general.' Nigel Manning, chairman of Ash Parish Council, remarked: 'To my mind, it’s “buyer beware.” You can’t really miss the clock—it’s 90 feet tall and right next door.' Pickles stated: 'Too many town halls have been over-zealous in trying to silence church bells and village clocks which have chimed for decades, if not centuries. We need common sense to recognize such sounds are part of the fabric of Britain’s life.' Tai maintains he was unaware of the chimes’ frequency when buying the house. 'We upgraded the double glazing and installed soundproofing—but it’s still not enough,' he said. 'I don’t think the chimes should continue after 11pm.'

article_content: By Daily Mail Reporter. PUBLISHED: 00:06 EST, 12 July 2013. | UPDATED: 00:06 EST, 12 July 2013. From faded flags painted on buildings to large ones that nearly engulf their proud bearers, the Stars and Stripes has become a common sight across the U.S. Photographer Shannon Davis began documenting how the flag has become woven into the fabric of American life by photographing it in her hometown of Buffalo and other parts of the country. She first noticed the prevalence of flags after returning to the U.S. following four years living in Britain. Face of America: A boy holds the Stars and Stripes in North Litchfield, South Carolina. Part of the furniture: A flag sticks out from the side of a chair in West Virginia. 'The more I looked, the more I saw that people display it every single day in these casual ways—but it almost seemed more real, personal, and in touch with what it means to be American,' she told CNN. As she began her 'Random Acts of Pride' project, Ms. Davis noticed flags in unexpected places—on the sides of barns, taped to cash registers, or hanging from fences. These displays occurred daily, not just during holidays like July 4th. 'Don’t they realize they’re trying to be patriotic, but they’re doing it in kind of a disheveled way?' she found herself thinking. Although people are usually absent in her photos, when they appear, they often become the emotional center of the image. Street art: The American flag stands out against graffiti in New York. Token: A small flag is taped to a cash register in a Los Angeles shop. Clinging on: A poster featuring the flag hangs from the side of a building in West Virginia. On one occasion, while photographing a flag outside a house, a neighbor across the street approached to ask what she was doing. After she explained her project, the man revealed he always kept a flag outside his home but had taken it down due to snow. He rushed inside to retrieve it. 'It’s ironic. It’s the same flag, but he wanted to get his flag,' Ms. Davis said. 'I just love that—that connection every person displaying the flag seems to have: It’s deeply personal to them.' Shelter: A large, weather-beaten flag is tacked to a barn in West Virginia. Hidden: The flag is barely visible among trees in an Atlanta photo. Borders: The remnants of a flag hang from a fence in Buffalo, New York. Faded glory: Only a few stars remain on a flag spotted along Highway 521 in South Carolina. The photographer, formerly the creative director for Turner Classic Movies advertisements celebrating classic films, noted that the flag’s placement often mirrors its surroundings. 'There are joyful, ironic, and playful moments—and others that are subtle, lonely, and detached. The flag isn’t always this shining, proud beacon. Sometimes, it looks lonely to me, and I wanted to capture that loneliness,' she said. Her project, visible on Visual 64, is not driven by patriotism but by a desire to document overlooked moments in everyday American life. Ms. Davis, who has also directed films, continues to expand 'Random Acts of Pride' as she travels across the U.S. All American: A boy idly plays with a flag in a Buffalo diner. Pride: When a homeowner learned of Shannon Davis’s project, he proudly displayed his flag. Reflections: The Stars and Stripes adorn a window in Buffalo. Citizenship: Three flags rest in a window beside election campaign posters. Tatters: This star-spangled banner in Atlanta appears battered by time and weather. Arrivals: Passengers at Buffalo Airport seem unaware of the two flags draped above them. Welcome sight: The Stars and Stripes appear in both windows of a New York State shop. Fashion: A mannequin wearing leggings obscures a flag hanging outside an Atlanta shop. Slogan: The stripes on this flag have been replaced with patriotic phrases. Standing guard: The Stars and Stripes flank a doorway with the words 'We Closed' painted above it in New York. Wash out: A woman waits for her laundry in Buffalo as a flag hangs high above her. In the shadows: A small flag flutters nearly unseen beneath a New York fire escape. Melting pot: The American flag contrasts sharply against a foreign goods store in Los Angeles. Have a nice day: Two iconic American images stand side by side. Eye-catching: The bold colors of the flag disrupt the monotony of a New York building. Strong foundations: Though this Atlanta home is unfinished, the flagpole is already in place.

He is now poised to make his official Premier League debut against Aston Villa on September 13. article_content: A former top-secret naval communications base in Wales — Criggion Station — has been sold to four local investors for regeneration. Used during World War II and the Cold War, the site transmitted critical military orders, including those that led to the sinking of the German battleship Bismarck in 1941 and the Argentine cruiser General Belgrano in 1982. Established in 1943, Criggion was built as a secure alternative after a fire destroyed the UK’s main communications hub in Rugby, Warwickshire. Its remote location and powerful transmitters made it vital for coordinating global Royal Navy operations. During the Cold War, the station became a nerve center for submarine communications, particularly during the Cuban Missile Crisis. With 160 personnel on-site in the 1960s, it was considered a prime target for Soviet nuclear strikes. The site was decommissioned in the late 1990s. In 2003, its three towering 700-foot radio masts and six additional structures were demolished, leaving behind four decaying buildings on 11.68 acres of land. Now, with renewed interest from the community, the property has been acquired by four local investors. Proposals under consideration include converting the buildings into a war museum, residential units, industrial storage, or a design studio. Powys County Councillor Graham Brown, who has long championed its preservation, emphasized its global significance: 'These buildings were linked to Hawaii and Colorado. Orders to sink the Bismarck — and later the General Belgrano — were believed to have been transmitted from here. This isn’t just local history; it’s world history.' While full sale details remain undisclosed, Telereal Trillium, the commercial real estate agent handling the transaction, noted strong community engagement and expressed confidence that regeneration will revitalise the area economically and culturally.

article_content: Dramatic images emerged today of a tornado-like cloud formation swirling in the skies off the coast of West Sussex. Stunned witnesses described seeing a massive funnel cloud over the English Channel near the seaside town of Selsey around 7:15 p.m. Coastguards launched a lifeboat as a precaution, but no distress signal was received. Father-of-two Carey Mackinnon, a Coastguard watch manager, photographed the phenomenon. Twisting cloud formations like this only qualify as tornadoes if they make contact with the ground; over water, they are typically classified as waterspouts. Despite their name, waterspouts do not suck up water — the visible column consists of water droplets formed by condensation. Mackinnon, 57, was driving from Chichester to Selsey to deliver lighting equipment when he spotted the formation. 'It was an incredible sight — something I’ve never seen before in England,' he said. 'I’ve seen them on TV, of course, but never here.' He pulled over to take photos, then parked near the lifeboat station for better vantage points. 'It looked like water was being drawn upward — as if thousands of gallons were being lifted into the cloud.' 'I saw a cruise ship heading toward it — the passengers must have had an unforgettable view.' Selsey has been struck by tornadoes before: in January 1998, one damaged around 1,000 buildings, causing an estimated £10 million in damage — roofs were torn off, walls and fences toppled, and trees uprooted. The 1998 tornado also destroyed the observatory of celebrity astronomer Patrick Moore, who resides in the town. A previous tornado hit Selsey in 1986, damaging approximately 200 homes and carving a path 70 meters wide.

article_content: The cast of Friends has said they are 'utterly devastated' by the loss of their fellow star Matthew Perry, who died on Saturday at the age of 54. In a joint statement, Jennifer Aniston, Courteney Cox, Matt LeBlanc, David Schwimmer, and Lisa Kudrow called it an 'unfathomable loss.' The actor was reportedly found unresponsive in a hot tub at his Los Angeles home on Saturday. His post-mortem examination was inconclusive; officials are awaiting the results of toxicology tests. 'We are all so utterly devastated by the loss of Matthew,' the Friends cast said in a statement released to the BBC. 'We were more than just castmates—we are a family. There is so much to say, but right now we’re going to take a moment to grieve and process this unfathomable loss. In time, we will say more, as and when we are able. For now, our thoughts and our love are with Matty’s family, his friends, and everyone who loved him around the world.' Perry was best known for playing the wisecracking Chandler Bing in the hugely popular 1990s TV sitcom. He also appeared in numerous films. Salma Hayek, who starred with Perry in the 1997 film Fools Rush In, shared a heartfelt tribute on Instagram, recalling their bond and calling the film 'probably my best movie.' Hayek added: 'Throughout the years, he and I found ourselves reminiscing about that meaningful time in our lives with a deep sense of nostalgia and gratitude. My friend, you are gone much too soon, but I will continue to cherish your silliness, your perseverance, and your lovely heart. Farewell, sweet Matthew—we will never forget you.' Perry’s former fiancée, Molly Hurwitz, reflected on watching Friends with him as he prepared for the 2021 cast reunion: 'Being with him as he rediscovered his brilliance was magical. He would love that the world is talking about how talented he was—and he really was very talented.' She continued: 'But I obviously knew that man in a very different way, too. While I loved him deeper than I could comprehend, he was complicated and caused pain like I’d never known. No one in my adult life has had a more profound impact on me than Matthew Langford Perry. I have tremendous gratitude for that—for everything I learned from our relationship.' Hurwitz also acknowledged the role of Alcoholics Anonymous (AA), concluding: 'I feel relief that you are at peace.' At the height of his fame, Perry struggled with addiction to painkillers and alcohol, entering rehab multiple times. In 2016, he told BBC Radio 2 that he could not remember three years of filming Friends due to substance use. The Los Angeles Fire Department confirmed Perry was found deceased in the jacuzzi at his Pacific Palisades home. A bystander had already repositioned him to clear his airway before responders arrived. Firefighters performed a quick medical assessment and confirmed he was deceased. Actor Hank Azaria, who appeared in several Friends episodes as Phoebe’s boyfriend David, described Perry as a 'brother.' In an Instagram video, he recalled meeting Perry at age 21 while Perry was 16, saying: 'We did a pilot together... we became really good friends and were more like brothers for a long time.' Azaria added: 'From a recovery perspective—I’ve been sober for 17 years. I want to say that the night I went into AA, Matthew brought me in. The whole first year I was sober, we went to meetings together. He was so caring, giving, and wise—he helped me get sober.' Lindsay Posner, who directed Perry’s 2016 play The End of Longing—written by and starring Perry—paid tribute on BBC Radio 4’s Today programme: 'He was always very warm and generous, and keen to keep everyone entertained. He wanted to be seen as both a serious and comic actor.' The play drew from Perry’s own battles with addiction. Posner noted: 'He said to me he would like to be remembered for helping people through the play… helping people to recover.' Kathleen Turner, who played Chandler’s mother on Friends, told People magazine: 'He had a good sense of humor and a good heart. He liked other people—which, to me, is terribly important, especially for an actor.' Fans gathered outside the Friends apartment building in New York to leave floral tributes. 'He’s had a very impactful role in my life and always gave me tons of laughs—it’s sad to hear about his passing,' said 26-year-old Taylor Lanthier. 'Chandler is a funny guy, a loving guy, someone devoted to his friends—and that’s what I think Matthew was too.' Tributes poured in over the weekend from Gwyneth Paltrow, Friends creators Marta Kauffman and David Crane, and Maggie Wheeler, who portrayed Janice.

Lindsay Posner, che ha diretto il dramma del 2016 The End of Longing—scritto e interpretato da Perry—ha reso omaggio su BBC Radio 4 Today: 'Era sempre molto caldo e generoso, e desiderava intrattenere tutti costantemente. I fan si sono radunati davanti all'edificio delle riprese di Friends a New York per lasciare omaggi floreali. 'Ha avuto un impatto enorme sulla mia vita e mi ha sempre fatto ridere tantissimo—è triste sentire della sua scomparsa,' ha detto Taylor Lanthier, 26 anni. article_content: Ransom demands are as old as kidnapping itself — but they never lose their power to shock, as the Japanese government has recently learned. In a video posted to social media on Tuesday, a black-clad ISIS militant stood over two men he claimed were Japanese citizens, threatening to execute them unless the Japanese government paid $200 million within 72 hours. While ISIS seeking ransom is not surprising, the public nature and extraordinary sum of this demand stand out. Although militant groups frequently kidnap for money, they rarely broadcast their demands so openly. One documented case is that of James Foley, an American journalist kidnapped in northern Syria in November 2012. ISIS later demanded $132 million (100 million euros) for his release, according to Richard Byrne, a spokesperson for GlobalPost, where Foley worked as a freelancer. Neither GlobalPost, Foley’s family, nor the U.S. government paid the ransom. Regardless, ISIS still beheaded him — and filmed the act for global distribution. What makes this latest demand unusual is its public timing and ultimatum — suggesting ISIS aims less for payment and more for psychological impact. The group criticized Japan for supporting governments involved in the anti-ISIS campaign, even though Tokyo is not part of the U.S.-led military coalition. Ransom payments serve dual purposes: funding operations and sending messages of terror. The U.S. Treasury estimated that al-Qaeda and its affiliates collected $120 million in ransoms over eight years through 2012. A 2014 New York Times investigation found that al-Qaeda affiliates received $125 million since 2008 — including $66 million in 2013 alone. While no comparable study exists for ISIS, experts agree ransoms are a major revenue stream alongside oil sales, taxation, and criminal activity. Countries rarely disclose ransom payments, fearing they will encourage more abductions. Yet evidence suggests otherwise. According to the New York Times, France has paid the most — approximately $58 million since 2008 — far exceeding payments from Oman ($20 million), Qatar ($20 million), Switzerland ($12 million), Spain ($11 million), and Austria ($3 million). Ransom amounts have surged over the past decade. A decade ago, demands averaged around $200,000; today, they often reach millions. Phil Balboni, CEO of GlobalPost, told CNN that European governments have paid between $2 million and $4 million per hostage — still far below the $132 million asked for Foley or the current $200 million demand. Japan has long maintained a firm no-ransom policy. In 2013, it endorsed a G8 declaration stating: 'We unequivocally reject the payment of ransoms to terrorists.' This aligns with the positions of the United States and United Kingdom. Diane Foley, James’s mother, recalled a U.S. official warning her that raising ransom funds could lead to prosecution. Why not pay? First, there’s no guarantee ISIS would honor the deal. Second, paying fuels future kidnappings. As David S. Cohen, then Under Secretary for Terrorism and Financial Intelligence, warned in 2012: 'Ransom payments lead to future kidnappings, and future kidnappings lead to additional ransom payments — building the capacity of terrorist organizations to conduct attacks.' The debate intensified after the U.S. exchanged five Taliban detainees for U.S. Army Sgt. Bowe Bergdahl in 2014. President Obama defended the move: 'I make absolutely no apologies for making sure we get a young man back to his parents.' But Japan has no such leverage — it holds no known ISIS suspects. Its only potential bargaining chip may be refraining from supporting anti-ISIS coalitions — a stance Prime Minister Abe has refused to abandon. Though talks may occur, Japan’s best hope for rescuing its citizens lies in military intervention by Western or regional allies. Time is running out.

Sebbene non sia sorprendente che l'ISIS chieda un riscatto, la natura pubblica e la somma straordinaria di questa richiesta si distinguono. Anche se i gruppi militanti sequestrano spesso per denaro, raramente rendono pubbliche le loro richieste in modo così aperto. Un caso documentato è quello di James Foley, un giornalista americano rapito nel nord della Siria nel novembre 2012. L'ISIS ha successivamente chiesto 132 milioni di dollari (100 milioni di euro) per il suo rilascio, secondo Richard Byrne, portavoce di GlobalPost, dove Foley lavorava come freelance. Né GlobalPost, né la famiglia di Foley, né il governo degli Stati Uniti hanno pagato il riscatto. Nonostante ciò, l'ISIS lo ha comunque decapitato — e ha diffuso il filmato dell'omicidio a livello globale. Ciò che rende questa ultima richiesta insolita è il suo carattere pubblico e l'ultimatum — suggerendo che l'ISIS miri meno al pagamento e più all'impatto psicologico. Il gruppo ha criticato il Giappone per aver sostenuto governi coinvolti nella campagna contro l'ISIS, anche se Tokyo non fa parte della coalizione militare guidata dagli Stati Uniti. I pagamenti di riscatto servono a duplice scopo: finanziare le operazioni e trasmettere messaggi di terrore. Il Dipartimento del Tesoro degli Stati Uniti ha stimato che al-Qaeda e i suoi affiliati hanno raccolto 120 milioni di dollari in riscatti negli otto anni fino al 2012. Un'indagine del New York Times del 2014 ha rilevato che gli affiliati di al-Qaeda hanno incassato 125 milioni di dollari dal 2008 — inclusi 66 milioni di dollari nel solo 2013. Sebbene non esista uno studio comparabile per l'ISIS, gli esperti concordano che i riscatti sono una fonte di reddito fondamentale insieme alle vendite di petrolio, tasse e attività criminali. I paesi raramente divulghino i pagamenti di riscatto, temendo di incoraggiare ulteriori rapimenti. Tuttavia, le prove suggeriscono il contrario. Secondo il New York Times, la Francia ha pagato di più — circa 58 milioni di dollari dal 2008 — ben oltre i pagamenti di Oman (20 milioni di dollari), Qatar (20 milioni di dollari), Svizzera (12 milioni di dollari), Spagna (11 milioni di dollari) e Austria (3 milioni di dollari). Le cifre richieste per i riscatti sono aumentate notevolmente negli ultimi dieci anni. Dieci anni fa, le richieste medie erano intorno ai 200.000 dollari; oggi spesso raggiungono i milioni. Phil Balboni, amministratore delegato di GlobalPost, ha dichiarato alla CNN che i governi europei hanno pagato tra 2 e 4 milioni di dollari per ogni ostaggio — ancora molto lontani dai 132 milioni richiesti per Foley o dai 200 milioni attuali. Il Giappone ha da tempo mantenuto una ferma politica di non pagamento dei riscatti. Nel 2013 ha sostenuto una dichiarazione del G8 che affermava: 'Rifiutiamo categoricamente il pagamento di riscatti ai terroristi.' Questo allinea la sua posizione con quella degli Stati Uniti e del Regno Unito. Diane Foley, madre di James, ha ricordato che un funzionario statunitense le aveva avvertito che raccogliere fondi per un riscatto poteva portare a un'accusa penale. Perché non pagare? Primo, non c'è garanzia che l'ISIS onorerà l'accordo. Secondo, pagare alimenta futuri rapimenti. Come ha avvertito David S. Cohen, allora Sottosegretario per il Terrorismo e l'Intelligence Finanziaria, nel 2012: 'I pagamenti di riscatto portano a futuri rapimenti, e i futuri rapimenti portano a ulteriori pagamenti di riscatto — costruendo la capacità delle organizzazioni terroristiche di compiere attacchi.' Il dibattito si è intensificato dopo lo scambio degli Stati Uniti di cinque detenuti talebani per il soldato dell'esercito americano Bowe Bergdahl nel 2014. Il presidente Obama ha difeso l'operazione: 'Non mi scuso affatto per assicurarmi che un giovane torni dai suoi genitori.' Ma il Giappone non ha questo tipo di leve — non detiene sospetti membri noti dell'ISIS. La sua unica carta possibile potrebbe essere astenersi dal sostenere le coalizioni anti-ISIS — una posizione che il primo ministro Abe si è rifiutato di abbandonare. Anche se potrebbero verificarsi colloqui, la migliore speranza del Giappone per salvare i propri cittadini risiede nell'intervento militare da parte di alleati occidentali o regionali. Il tempo sta per scadere.

article_content: While most photos today are digital, there was a time when sepia-toned hard copies were considered precious relics — and families would eagerly cherish any they received from the past. Some lucky families recently had that experience, thanks to the efforts of one man in St. Louis County, Minnesota. When Matt Seppo, facilities supervisor at the Chris Jensen Nursing Home, stumbled upon bags of old photographs while cleaning in 2005, he could have easily discarded them with the trash. But he didn’t. A self-described history enthusiast and amateur genealogist, Seppo had long been passionate about old images. 'I’m a collector,' he told HLN. 'For years, I collected vintage military memorabilia. My interest in genealogy began when my grandmother passed down a photo album from the 1860s.' Seppo had traced his own family roots to Finland, arriving in the U.S. in the mid-1800s. So when he found the nursing home photos, he took on the mission of returning them to their rightful owners — or at least their living descendants. But how do you trace photos decades old? 'I started by turning them face-down and feeling the paper thickness to group them,' Seppo explained. 'I also used postmarks to estimate when and where they were developed.' He supplemented his research with phone books, newspaper archives, U.S. Census records, and the genealogy database of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. After holding onto the photos for eight years, Seppo finally found a breakthrough in November. 'The big moment was when I found people who actually belonged to these photos,' he said. 'I did it all myself. I used Google for some research — though I’m the last person on earth to own a cell phone or a computer,' he laughed. The bags held around 150 photographs, some dating as far back as 1890. One man — whom Seppo described as 'very distinctive' — appeared repeatedly, from infancy to adulthood. His name, La Verne Swenson, was written on one of the storage bags, but no connection to the nursing home was evident. 'I tracked down La Verne’s brother and sister through research in Wisconsin,' Seppo said. 'I found a newspaper clipping that suggested Julie Swenson was married to a man related to La Verne. It turned out La Verne’s sister Lillian and brother Olaf had a child — Eugene — who became Julie’s husband.' The Swensons weren’t the only family Seppo reunited with photos. He also located the Hunter family in Cloquet, Minnesota, and delivered images of Mickey Hunter’s great-great-grandfather — someone Mickey had never seen before. 'You know more about my family than I do,' Hunter told Seppo during their first meeting. He was right: Seppo had identified the ancestor by cross-referencing a World War I draft registration form and tracing descendants. Though many photos remain unclaimed, Seppo says he’s deeply fulfilled by the connections he’s already made.

Alcune famiglie fortunatissime hanno recentemente vissuto questa esperienza, grazie agli sforzi di un uomo della Contea di St. Louis, nel Minnesota. Quando Matt Seppo, supervisore delle strutture presso la Chris Jensen Nursing Home, ha trovato sacchi di vecchie fotografie durante una pulizia nel 2005, poteva facilmente buttarle via con la spazzatura. Ma non lo ha fatto. Un appassionato di storia e genealogista dilettante, Seppo da anni coltivava una passione per le immagini antiche. 'Sono un collezionista,' ha detto a HLN. 'Per anni ho raccolto memorabilia militari d’epoca. Il mio interesse per la genealogia è nato quando mia nonna mi ha lasciato un album fotografico degli anni ’60 del XIX secolo.' Seppo aveva tracciato le proprie radici familiari fino alla Finlandia, arrivata negli Stati Uniti nella metà del 1800. Così, quando ha trovato le foto dell’ospizio, si è impegnato nel compito di restituirle ai legittimi proprietari — o almeno ai loro discendenti viventi. Ma come si rintracciano foto che risalgono a decenni fa? 'Ho iniziato girandole a faccia in giù e sentendo lo spessore della carta per raggrupparle,' ha spiegato Seppo. 'Ho anche usato i bolli postali per stimare quando e dove sono state sviluppate.' Ha integrato la sua ricerca con elenchi telefonici, archivi di giornali, registri del censimento americano e il database genealogico della Chiesa di Gesù Cristo dei Santi degli Ultimi Giorni. Dopo aver conservato le foto per otto anni, Seppo ha finalmente trovato una svolta a novembre. 'Il momento decisivo è stato quando ho trovato persone che effettivamente appartenevano a queste foto,' ha detto. 'L’ho fatto tutto da solo. Ho usato Google per alcune ricerche — anche se sono l’ultima persona sulla terra ad avere un cellulare o un computer,' ha scherzato. I sacchi contenevano circa 150 fotografie, alcune datate addirittura al 1890. Un uomo — che Seppo descrive come 'molto distintivo' — appariva ripetutamente, dall’infanzia all’età adulta. 'Ho rintracciato il fratello e la sorella di La Verne attraverso ricerche in Wisconsin,' ha detto Seppo. 'Ho trovato un articolo di giornale che suggeriva che Julie Swenson fosse sposata con un uomo legato a La Verne. In realtà, la sorella di La Verne, Lillian, e il fratello Olaf avevano un figlio — Eugene — che è diventato il marito di Julie.' I Swenson non sono stati l’unica famiglia che Seppo ha ricongiunto alle foto. Ha anche localizzato la famiglia Hunter a Cloquet, nel Minnesota, e consegnato a Mickey Hunter immagini del suo bis-bisnonno, qualcuno che Mickey non aveva mai visto prima. 'Mi conosci più della mia stessa famiglia,' ha detto Hunter a Seppo durante il loro primo incontro. Aveva ragione: Seppo aveva identificato l’antenato incrociando un modulo di registrazione alla coscrizione della Prima Guerra Mondiale e tracciando i discendenti. Sebbene molte foto rimangano ancora da assegnare, Seppo dice di sentirsi profondamente soddisfatto dai legami già stabiliti.
